text: One deed by itself did little.
The power came from numbers.
Neighbors signed in blocs, often pledging a set share of a block's frontage before the agreement took effect, so a single signed covenant could seal off whole streets at once.
A standard printed form circulated so any block could adopt one.
A Chicago attorney named Nathan MacChesney drafted a model covenant in 1927 that real estate boards handed out across the city.
Beginning in the late 1920s, covenants swept across the white neighborhoods ringing the Black Belt, including Kenwood, Oakland, Hyde Park, Woodlawn, and Englewood.
By the 1940s, hundreds of subdivisions across Cook County carried them.
And the University of Chicago was not a bystander to this.
From 1933 to 1947, the university spent more than 110,000 dollars on what it politely called community interests.
More than 83,000 of those dollars went specifically to defending restrictive covenants in the blocks around its campus.
The Chicago Defender had a blunter name for the whole arrangement.
The paper called the covenants the University of Chicago Agreement to get rid of Negroes.
The covenants were rarely beaten head-on, because the law was on their side.
The Hansberry family came closest.
Carl Hansberry, a real estate man himself, bought a home at 6140 South Rhodes Avenue in Woodlawn in the spring of 1937 and moved his family in that June.
His daughter Lorraine was a young child.
A white neighbor, Anna Lee, and the Woodlawn Property Owners Association went to court to enforce a covenant and drive the family out.
A mob gathered outside.
A brick came through a window and nearly struck Lorraine.
The fight went all the way to the Supreme Court.
In Hansberry versus Lee, decided November 12, 1940, the Court ruled in the family's favor.
But it ruled on a narrow procedural point, namely that an earlier lawsuit could not legally bind him.
It did not touch the covenants themselves, and it did not say they were unconstitutional.
Lorraine Hansberry would later turn the family's ordeal into the play A Raisin in the Sun.
